I used to think stories were something you consumed—like food you devoured quickly, then forgot in the rush of daily life. But lately I’ve begun to suspect stories are more like weather. They arrive on their own schedule. They soak into your clothes without asking permission. They leave behind a dampness you don’t notice until you try to move through the day and your thoughts feel heavy, slower, strangely burdened with atmosphere.

Lately I’ve been thinking about how stories start.

Some start with a sentence that snaps like a hook: *It was the kind of night you couldn’t forget.* Others begin with a question so casual it sounds like conversation: *Have you ever wondered what happens to the things we lose?* And some begin without permission at all—an image you can’t explain, a sound that echoes after you’ve stopped hearing it, a name you haven’t spoken in years that suddenly feels lodged behind your teeth.

I don’t know which kind I’m in the mood for. I only know I’m in the mood for something honest, something that doesn’t pretend to be tidy. Because the world is not tidy. The world is a cabinet with drawers that don’t match. The world is a bucket with holes in it. The world is—if we’re being truthful—an ongoing draft.

There’s a particular kind of story that grows in the gaps between what people say and what they mean. Those stories aren’t written down so much as lived. You can feel them the way you feel a change in pressure before a storm: a shift in the air, an extra beat before someone answers, an effort to change the subject like turning your body away from a cold breeze.

In those gaps, details matter. The way someone laughs too quickly. The way a hand pauses above a cup and then decides to set the cup down with extra care. The way a person says they’re “fine” but their eyes look somewhere else. If you pay attention to those things, you start to realize how much storytelling happens without an audience. People tell stories all the time; they just don’t always know they’re narrators. They edit their own experiences as they speak, trimming the parts that make them look too human, too frightened, too unprepared.

And yet—every now and then—someone drops the mask. Not in a dramatic, cinematic way. It’s smaller. It’s like a seam you only notice after you’ve looked at it long enough. They say one sentence that accidentally reveals the whole structure: *I keep expecting him to come back, even though I know it’s been years.* Or: *I thought if I became useful enough, I wouldn’t be left.* Or: *I don’t know how to stop replaying it.*

When that happens, the room changes.

That’s the thing about stories: they don’t just entertain. They rearrange. They make you sit differently in your chair. They make you aware of the distance between your life and someone else’s life, and at the same time they collapse that distance, because you realize you’ve felt a version of the same thing, maybe under a different name.

I think that’s why I’m drawn to writing—because writing is one of the few places where rearrangement is allowed. You can take the chaos of experience and reframe it so the chaos makes a strange kind of sense. Not always a “happy” sense. Not always a “moral” sense. But a sense.

When I write, I’m always surprised by what I’m willing to admit. It begins with ordinary material: a street corner, a kitchen light, a late afternoon that feels like it should be temporary but refuses to be. Then the words come—sometimes gentle, sometimes ruthless—and suddenly I’m standing inside a memory I didn’t realize I was carrying. I’m not watching it from the outside; I’m inside it, as if I’m again the person who first learned whatever lesson that memory contains.

People talk about inspiration like it’s lightning. They say you wait for it, chase it, pray for it. But for me inspiration is less like a bolt and more like an ember. It appears slowly, in the background. I have to keep returning to the question: what am I actually trying to say? What am I avoiding? What detail feels too specific to be accidental?

Sometimes the answer is buried in something mundane. The smell of a particular soap. The weight of a winter coat that never quite warms up. The sound of a radiator that rattles in a way that almost sounds like language if you’re tired enough.

Other times the answer is in a pattern. The way I keep writing about doors that don’t open, or about people who arrive late, or about the moment right before something breaks. I notice these patterns not because they’re obvious, but because they keep returning like a refrain in a song you can’t stop hearing once you’ve recognized it.

Maybe that’s what art is: recognition. A mirror held at an angle that catches the light and shows you something you thought you didn’t have. The best stories make recognition feel like a revelation rather than a diagnosis. They don’t say, “This is what you are.” They say, “This is what you already know, but you haven’t met yet.”

In real life, we rarely get that kind of clarity. Real life keeps its secrets. It makes you wait. It makes you live with unanswered questions. It makes you carry the unsaid.

I’ve been noticing, too, how people treat endings.

Some endings are dramatic—goodbyes that take place with boxes and paperwork and sudden tears. But most endings are quiet. They are a gradual dimming of attention. A delayed reply that becomes a habit. A friendship that stops feeling mutual. A promise that grows thin like paper. An old joy that begins to feel like an obligation.

We don’t mark those endings the way we mark anniversaries. We simply absorb the change and call it “moving on,” as if grief can be replaced with a strategy.

But stories can honor endings. Stories can say: *This mattered.* Stories can hold the ache long enough for it to become something you can name without being crushed by it.

I’ve also learned that stories can be dangerous.

A good story convinces you to believe. It persuades you to step into another person’s skin. It invites you to grant empathy where you might otherwise withhold it. That’s a gift, but it can also be a trap, because you can start believing in the narrative you prefer rather than the reality you’re actually in.

There are stories that claim to explain everything. There are stories that reduce people to villains and saints, neat categories that keep you from having to do the harder work of seeing complexity. Those stories spread easily because they comfort you. They make the world feel legible. They reassure you that if you just choose the right side, you’ll never be surprised again.

But life surprises you anyway.

So maybe the best approach is to write stories that don’t pretend to be omniscient. Stories that allow themselves to be wrong. Stories that admit uncertainty without drowning in it. Stories that can say, *I don’t know,* and then continue.

There’s a particular kind of honesty in that phrase—an honesty that makes room for both regret and possibility. Because even if you can’t correct the past, you can still decide how to carry it. You can still decide what you do next.

Lately, I’ve found myself wanting to write about return.

Not literal return, though sometimes that happens in stories—people come back, places open again, lost items reappear like miracles. But I mean return in the emotional sense. The act of going back into yourself and finding something you left there. The act of admitting that you’re not finished being the person you were.

I think we underestimate how often people return. We return to old songs. We return to old fears. We return to certain types of love and certain types of mistakes because they feel familiar, and familiarity can masquerade as safety. We return to the same question with different wording: *How do I stop hurting myself?* *How do I forgive?* *How do I begin again without pretending I’m not carrying what I’ve lost?*

And maybe the role of a story is not to answer those questions conclusively, but to keep them company.

To sit beside them when they’re quiet. To hold them up to the light and say, “Look. This is what it feels like.” To make the invisible visible. To translate private storms into shared language.

When I write freely, when I don’t force a plot to behave, I feel like I’m walking through a house I’ve lived in all my life but never explored. Rooms appear with doors I don’t remember. Corners hold furniture I didn’t place. There are photographs on the wall that I recognize only in fragments—the curve of a smile, the shadow behind an eye, the timestamp in the corner that doesn’t match the way I remember time moving.

At some point, I stop trying to map it perfectly. I just move through. I let myself be guided by feeling. I let the words lead me where my mind would rather avoid.

And if I’m lucky, the story—this improvised weather—changes me while it’s happening.

It leaves behind something like a new air pressure. A slightly different horizon. The sense that I can look at my life and see it as material rather than fate. Not as something fixed, but as something narrated—something that can be revised, gently, with care.

Perhaps that’s what I want from stories most: not escape, not distraction, not neat closure.

I want them to be a way back. A way to return to myself with a little more clarity. A way to acknowledge the ache without turning it into a cage. A way to make meaning out of the messy draft of being human.

So I’ll keep writing—freely, imperfectly, like weather rolling in—until the room feels different and I can breathe again.
